extracted.intended_audience: students, policymakers, and readers of political economy / economic history
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes Adam Smith's stated causes and impediments to the prosperity of new colonies — the economic, legal, and institutional conditions he identifies as promoting or hindering colonial wealth, population, and improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenty of good land
rubrics_metrics.description: Plenty of good land ... are the two great causes of the prosperity of all new colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith repeatedly identifies the ready availability of extensive, fertile, and cheap land as a primary cause of rapid progress: "Every colonist gets more land than he can possibly cultivate... He has every motive to render as great as possible a produce which is thus to be almost entirely his own." Plenty of land reduces rents, raises the marginal return to labour applied to improvement, and underpins high wages, population growth, and investment in cultivation and local improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty to manage their own affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty to manage their own affairs their own way, seem to be the two great causes of the prosperity of all new colonies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and administrative autonomy (or sufficient distance from the mother country to allow practical autonomy) lets colonists pursue locally advantageous policies. Smith contrasts English colonies' greater freedom in management with the more controlling, expensive, or ceremonial governance of Spain, Portugal, and (at times) France, and credits local liberty with enabling faster improvement and cultivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint on engrossing uncultivated land; obligation to improve
rubrics_metrics.description: The engrossing of uncultivated land ... has been more restrained in the English colonies than in any other. The colony law, which imposes upon every proprietor the obligation of improving and cultivating, within a limited time, a certain proportion of his lands ... has, however, had some effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal rules that prevent large tracts of waste land from being monopolized (engrossed) and that compel proprietors to improve land promote division, cultivation, and use of labour. Smith stresses that engrossing destroys the plenty and cheapness of good land and is the "greatest obstruction to its improvement." Colony laws that declare neglected land grantable to others are cited as a practical countermeasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance and tenure rules that facilitate division and alienation
rubrics_metrics.description: In Pennsylvania there is no right of primogeniture, and lands, like moveables, are divided equally among all the children ... the tenure of the lands, which are all held by free soccage, facilitates alienation; and the grantee of an extensive tract of land generally finds it for his interest to alienate ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that inheritance customs and land tenure which promote subdivision and ready alienation (e.g., no primogeniture; free soccage) prevent the permanent engrossing of large estates and speed redistribution of land to active cultivators. By contrast, entailed or noble tenures (majorazzo, chivalric tenures) impede alienation and retard improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: High wages of labour combined with cheap land encourage population and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The liberal reward of labour encourages marriage. The children ... are well fed and properly taken care of; and when they are grown up, the value of their labour greatly overpays their maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When land is plentiful and cheap, proprietors offer high wages to attract labour; those wages encourage household formation and higher population growth, and the value of labour applied to uncultivated land often yields returns that justify maintenance and later accumulation. Smith treats this wage/land-price dynamic as central to the virtuous cycle of population, improvement, and increased real wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of taxes and light civil government expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: In consequence of the moderation of their taxes, a greater proportion of this produce belongs to themselves, which they may store up and employ ... The expense of their own civil government has always been very moderate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low civil taxation and frugal colonial civil establishments leave more surplus produce in colonists' hands to save and invest (thus increasing capital and labour). Smith contrasts the small civil costs in English colonies with the heavier ceremonial and administrative expenditures in Spanish, Portuguese, and (sometimes) French colonial administrations, which he views as a drag on local accumulation and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mother country bearing defence cost can benefit colonies' civil affordability
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of their own civil government has always been very moderate. The most important part of the expense of government, indeed, that of defence and protection, has constantly fallen upon the mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith notes that when the mother country shoulders defence costs (fleets, armies), colonists' own civil burdens can remain light, facilitating accumulation. He warns, however, that defence expenses borne by the mother country are large relative to civil costs; the point is descriptive of fiscal allocation effects on colonial prosperity rather than prescriptive taxation policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ecclesiastical oppression (tithes, mendicant friars, clergy engrossing land)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the colonies of all those three nations [Spain, Portugal, France], too, the ecclesiastical government is extremely oppressive. Tithes take place in all of them, and are levied with the utmost rigour ... the clergy are, in all of them, the greatest engrossers of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith treats heavy ecclesiastical burdens—strict tithes, licensed mendicancy of friars, and large church landholdings—as onerous taxes on the poor and as a form of land engrossment that retards productive improvement. Reducing ecclesiastical exactions and limiting clerical land accumulation is thereby favorable to prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom in disposal of surplus produce; broad market access (avoid exclusive companies)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the disposal of their surplus produce ... the English colonies have been more favoured, and have been allowed a more extensive market, than those of any other European nation ... Some nations have given up the whole commerce of their colonies to an exclusive company ... Of all the expedients that can well be contrived to stunt the natural growth of a new colony, that of an exclusive company is undoubtedly the most effectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open access to markets and freedom for colonial producers to sell to multiple buyers (and to import goods) encourage production, discourage artificial suppression of output, and permit natural economic growth. Exclusive trading companies, monopolies, or restrictive mercantile practices dramatically depress colonial incentives to expand production; examples given include the Dutch and Danish companies and the beneficial effects of relaxing exclusive privileges (Dutch license example, Curacoa and Eustatia as free ports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remoteness/distance from the mother country (practical autonomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their great distance from Europe has in all of them alleviated more or less the effects of this dependency. Their situation has placed them less in the view, and less in the power of their mother country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geographic distance reduces direct oversight and the ability of the mother country to enforce restrictive or burdensome policies; practical autonomy can allow colonies to pursue policies better suited to local interest. Smith cites distance as one reason European colonies (especially English ones) could follow their own course and thus prosper despite formal dependency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extraordinary encouragement of mining/speculative ventures
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all those expensive and uncertain projects ... there is none, perhaps, more perfectly ruinous than the search after new silver and gold mines ... Projects of mining, instead of replacing the capital employed ... commonly absorb both capital and profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith warns that speculative mining ventures (searches for precious-metal mines) are extremely risky, frequently ruinous, and consume capital without providing commensurate returns; therefore a prudent lawgiver should not give them extraordinary encouragement or divert disproportionate capital toward them. This functions as a caution against policies that channel excessive public or private capital into high-risk mineral speculation.
